name: Boost.Context
baseline: glibc ucontext_t (makecontext/swapcontext) user-space context switch, built as Boost.Context's own context-impl=ucontext backend
workload: Round-trip context switch through callcc()/continuation, reported as the average per jump (two jumps per round trip) in nanoseconds and CPU cycles, release build.
claimed_speedup: fcontext_t (hand-written per-platform jump_fcontext/make_fcontext assembly): 9 ns / 19 CPU cycles per switch; ucontext_t: 547 ns / 1130 CPU cycles; Windows Fiber: 49 ns / 98 CPU cycles. Roughly 61x lower latency and 59x fewer cycles than ucontext_t (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1; b2 properties variant=release, optimization=speed (performance/callcc/Jamfile.v2 also sets link=static, threading=multi and -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS)
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: Hand-written assembly per ABI and OS: src/asm holds jump_, make_ and ontop_ files for x86_64, i386, arm, arm64, mips32/64, ppc32/64, riscv64, s390x, sparc64, loongarch64 and alpha across ELF, Mach-O, PE and XCOFF. Stackful switch only; the caller supplies or allocates stacks. ucontext and Windows Fiber backends remain selectable as portable fallbacks (context-impl feature).
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own doc table and were not re-run. Compiler flags are given as b2 build properties, not literal -O flags. The ucontext_t column's build recipe is inferred from build/Jamfile.v2 and boost-context-features.jam (context-impl=ucontext); the doc page does not say how that column was built. gcc-6.3.1 on a Broadwell-era Xeon, so the numbers are old. The baseline is glibc ucontext, which likely pays a signal-mask system call per swap (not broken down on the page), so the gap says little about assembly versus compiled C; a context switch cannot be written in portable C, so no -O3 C comparison exists. Other user-space switchers (libco, minicoro) are not compared. The assembly is only part of the repo; the benchmark harness is performance/callcc/performance.cpp and performance/fcontext/performance.cpp.
found_via: Hacker News: 10 WebSearch queries restricted to news.ycombinator.com (e.g. 'Show HN hand-written assembly faster than compiler -O3 memcpy strlen kernel', 'FFmpeg devs boast of another 100x leap thanks to handwritten assembly code') surfaced only projects already catalogued or without repos. Found by a coverage-gap check on hand-written assembly in C++ libraries; boostorg/context was absent from the known list.

name: crc32-vpmsum
baseline: slice-by-8 table-driven CRC32 in C (based on Linux kernel lib/crc32.c, shipped in the repo as slice_by_8_bench.c)
workload: CRC of a 32 kB buffer repeated 5,000,000 times so it stays L1 resident, timed with the shell 'time' on slice_by_8_bench and crc32_bench; plus a kernel-side btrfs write test to a ramdisk.
claimed_speedup: slice_by_8_bench 122.220 seconds versus crc32_bench 2.937 seconds, 'just over 41x faster', about 52 GiB/sec or 13.6 bytes/cycle on a 4.1 GHz POWER8; btrfs write performance 3.8x faster with the kernel version.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile default CFLAGS: -m64 -g -O2 -mcpu=power8 -mcrypto -mpower8-vector -maltivec -mvsx, static link; compiler and version not stated in the README. Makefile default polynomial CRC=0x11EDC6F41.
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; README says a version was added to the Linux kernel
tradeoffs: POWER8 or newer only (vpmsum instructions). Ships a pure-assembly version (crc32.S, barrett_reduction.S, final_fold*.S) and a C version using gcc vector intrinsics (vec_crc32.c). A constants header is generated per polynomial at build time. Not portable to x86 or ARM.
caveats: First-party numbers from a loop of 5,000,000 calls timed with 'time'; compiler version and exact POWER8 model unstated, so tier C although the benchmark source is public. The baseline is a table-driven C routine, not compiler auto-vectorized output (no auto-vectorized CRC is tested). The repo also offers an intrinsics version and the README gives no separate figure for it, so the win is not attributable to hand-written assembly versus C. Hardware is old and the repo has not been updated since 2020. Not found via Hacker News; the 41x figure is the README's own.
found_via: Hacker News: 10 WebSearch queries restricted to news.ycombinator.com returned only catalogued projects. Found by a coverage-gap check on vendor-ISA hand-written CRC kernels (POWER8 vpmsum); not surfaced by an HN thread.

name: libco (higan-emu)
language: C (hand-assembled machine-code context switch per CPU)
baseline: OS preemptive threads (kernel thread context switches)
workload: Cooperative user-space context switches per second versus kernel-scheduled preemptive threads, for servers and emulators needing very high switch rates.
claimed_speedup: 'libco can easily scale to 10,000,000 or more context switches per second' while applications needing '100,000 or more context switches per second' hit kernel overhead with preemptive threads (README claim, no measurements).
stars_or_usage: 183 stars; README names servers and emulators as ideal use cases
tradeoffs: Four-function C89 API (co_active, co_create, co_delete, co_switch); backends for x86, amd64, PowerPC, PowerPC64 ELFv1/ELFv2, ARM, AArch64, plus setjmp, ucontext and Windows fiber fallbacks. No safety checks by design. Single-core cooperative scheduling only. The amd64 backend writes the switch routine as a byte array of machine code (co_swap_function) made executable at runtime.
caveats: No benchmark code, methodology, compiler, hardware or measured numbers in the repo; the 10,000,000 switches per second figure is an assertion. The baseline is a class (OS threads), not a named library, so the entry is weak; keep as low-confidence and tier C at most. Not compared against ucontext, Boost.Context or other user-space switchers.
found_via: Hacker News: 10 WebSearch queries restricted to news.ycombinator.com returned no libco thread. Found by a coverage-gap check on user-space context switching with hand-written assembly, alongside Boost.Context.
